paras: The lynching of Frank Dupree took place near Forest Hill, Rapides Parish, Louisiana, in June 1903, when a mob took Dupree, a young Black man, from the officer carrying him to jail and hanged and shot him. Dupree had been arrested on the accusation that he killed J. M. Ditter, a white carpenter, at the Long Leaf mill on June 11. The case ran as a short wire story across the South and later appeared in the monthly lynching lists of both white and Black papers.

Ditter was head carpenter at the Crowell & Spencer sawmill at Long Leaf, about three miles north of Glenmora. The wire gave his age as 40 and said he left a wife and two children, while the Alexandria Town Talk put him at about 35 with "several children." The wire described Dupree as a "mulatto about 21 years of age"; Town Talk added that his employers claimed he was insane.

According to an Alexandria dispatch of June 12, at about four o'clock the previous afternoon Dupree slipped up behind Ditter, who was repairing a pile driver, and struck him on the head with a bar of iron, killing him. Town Talk's correspondent wrote that the two men had "no words at all" and that other Black and white men stopped the man's flight by threatening him with their adzes. An inquest was held on Ditter's body and Dupree was arrested.

While being taken to the jail at Alexandria, the prisoner was seized about three-quarters of a mile from Forest Hill. The wire said only that "the officer" was overpowered, while a New Orleans dispatch to the New York Sun said the deputy sheriffs in charge were stopped by a mob. Town Talk described "an enraged mob, about 150 armed men," which tied the man to a rope, swung him from a limb and riddled his body with bullets. The other accounts likewise say he was hanged to a tree and shot.

No report of an inquest on Dupree, of arrests among the mob or of a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage. Town Talk noted that this was the second Black man "tied and shot to death in this neighborhood" that year.

The Alexandria wire ran on June 13 in the Montgomery Advertiser, the Birmingham Age-Herald and the Savannah Morning News, and two days later in the Atlanta Constitution. Headlines put the race of each man forward: "Negro Who Killed White Man Falls in Hands of Mob" in Montgomery, "Partly Demented Negro Lynched" in New York. The Age-Herald's printing turned the wire's closing line into a claim that Ditter had killed Dupee's wife and two children, and headlined the story accordingly, although the other printings of the same text say only that Ditter left a wife and two children.

Condensed versions spread as one-line items in news digests, some of them placing the event in Alabama. In Louisiana, the Winnfield Southern Sentinel and the St. Landry Clarion carried brief notices. The New Iberia Enterprise reprinted Town Talk's fuller local report under the headline "White Man Killed by a Black Negro," which dismissed the employers' claim that the man was insane and reported the lynching without comment.

The Black press printed no account of its own. The Indianapolis Freeman entered "June 11—Frank Dupree, colored, Forest Hill, La." in its list of the month's lynchings, prefaced by the remark that June had sustained its reputation as a month of "fatalities, deaths, destructions." The Wichita Searchlight and the Seattle Republican ran the same entry in their lynching tallies, as did white papers such as the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic.

Accounts differ on the timing: the Alexandria wire of June 12 already reported the lynching and a South Carolina brief placed it on Thursday night, June 11, while the Ocala Banner said Friday and the Sun's dispatch of June 13 said "to-day." The local Glenmora report did not name the accused, and the Sun printed the dead man's name as "J. H. Dilter." The Sun called Dupree "partly demented," while Town Talk reported that his employers claimed he was insane but said that "he never showed insanity."

The Alexandria wire (A1, A2, A4), a separate New Orleans dispatch (A5) and the local Town Talk account (A13) agree on the killing of Ditter, the seizure near Forest Hill and the hanging and shooting.

framing.detail: The Age-Herald headed the wire 'NEGRO LYNCHED. He Slays White Man Who Killed His Wife and Children.', a reading no other printing supports.
The Montgomery Advertiser headlined 'Negro Who Killed White Man Falls in Hands of Mob' and reported the lynching without comment.
The New York Sun headlined 'Partly Demented Negro Lynched' and called the killing of Ditter an 'assassination'.
Town Talk's headline 'White Man Killed by a Black Negro' centered the white victim, rejected the insanity claim and reported the lynching without censure.
The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic listed the case under 'Number of Lynchings Increasing Throughout North and South'.
The Freeman listed Dupree among June's lynchings, introducing the list by saying June had 'sustained its reputation' as a month of fatalities; Black papers printed no account of their own.
